blurbs.introduction: What the course is, who it is for, a free org, and the first dataset loaded.
blurbs.foundations: What CRM Analytics is, the three layers, the vocabulary, and when it is the wrong tool.
blurbs.setup: Licences, permission sets, the integration user, security predicates and sharing inheritance.
blurbs.data-preparation: Connections, sync, recipes, buckets, missing values and de-duplication.
blurbs.datasets-and-modelling: Grain, joins and fan-out, snapshots for history, and field metadata.
blurbs.data-visualization: Every chart type on its own terms, and which one the question actually needs.
blurbs.lenses-and-explorations: Exploring a dataset: groupings, measures, the three modes, and conversational queries.
blurbs.saql: The query language itself — syntax, functions, the patterns that matter, and debugging.
blurbs.designing-dashboards: Designing for a decision: hierarchy, formatting, widgets and performance.
blurbs.interactions: Faceting, filters and selection — what makes a dashboard a system rather than a page.
blurbs.bindings: One widget feeding another: selection, results, nesting, and where it turns unmaintainable.
blurbs.dashboard-json: Under the hood: reading and editing the JSON when the builder runs out.
blurbs.collaboration: Apps and sharing, subscriptions, annotations, embedding and governance.
blurbs.apis-and-automation: The REST API, Python, automated dataset loads, and CI for analytics.
blurbs.einstein-discovery: Stories, models, writing predictions back — and auditing a score before trusting it.
blurbs.gtm-engineering: The warehouse, metric contracts, and the metric tree the builds fill in.
blurbs.demand-analytics: AI search visibility, SEO, acquisition, campaigns, spend and attribution.
blurbs.pipeline-analytics: Leads through to signature: routing, scoring, conversion, velocity and CPQ.
blurbs.revops-analytics: Forecast, the ARR waterfall, consumption risk, service, and the executive board.

header.title: Making CRM Analytics learnable for everyone
header.lead: Two things to know: what this project is, and who builds it.

project.title: Great analytics learning shouldn't be locked away
project.p1: Learning CRM Analytics usually means stitching together scattered docs, expensive courses, and out-of-date blog posts. The result is a steep, lonely climb — even though the platform is genuinely powerful once it clicks.
project.p2: {name} exists to fix that: one coherent, modern, community-driven curriculum that takes you from "what is a CRM?" all the way to deploying an explainable prediction back into Salesforce. It is, and always will be, free and open source.
project.p3: Everything is written in the open. Spot a mistake or want to add a recipe? Open a pull request — the curriculum gets better with every learner who joins in.

principles.title: Open, and free at the core
principles.desc: No sign-up wall. Most lessons are free and live in a public repo you can read, fork and improve; a few hands-on lessons are part of Pro.

principles.title: A path, not a pile
principles.desc: Nineteen sections build on each other — from what CRM Analytics is, through SAQL and dashboard design, to seventeen go-to-market dashboards on the Academy’s own business data.

principles.title: Hands-on by default
principles.desc: Real SAQL, recipes, and dashboard examples you can paste straight into your own org.

principles.title: AI-native
principles.desc: Every page is published as Markdown and over MCP, so assistants can teach from the source.

author.title: Built by one developer, for the whole community
author.p1: Hi — I'm {name}. I build on the Salesforce platform and care a lot about making hard things approachable. I started CRM Analytics Academy after watching too many capable people bounce off the learning curve, simply because the good material was scattered, dated, or behind a paywall.
author.p2: So I turned what I'd learned the hard way into a structured, open path others can follow — the resource I wish I'd had when I started. Every lesson is something I'd actually want a teammate to read on their first week.
author.p3: This is an ongoing, community-driven project. If it helped you, the best thanks is to {star}, suggest a topic, or contribute a lesson.

cta.body: It's free, open, and built to take you from CRM basics all the way to certified.

ways.intro: There are four main ways to help — pick whatever fits your time and skills:

write.label: Write or fix a lesson
write.text: improve wording, fix errors, or add a whole new lesson (Markdown, no coding needed).

translate.label: Translate
translate.text: bring a lesson or the UI into one of the site's languages.

resource.label: Suggest a resource
resource.text: share a great docs page, course, tool, or community. {link} — it goes into a moderation queue, not a GitHub issue.

code.label: Improve the code
code.text: fix a bug, refine the UI, or add a feature via a pull request.

ways.outro: Lesson and code changes go through GitHub, because every lesson is a file in the repo. Resources and lesson ideas are submitted on the site and reviewed in the admin console.

setup.checks: Before committing, always run the two checks (there's no test runner):
setup.tip: {label} if the docs sidebar ever looks empty in dev, the local content database went stale. Fix it with {cmd}.

lessons.p1: Lessons are plain Markdown under {path}. English lives in {en}. The number prefixes set the order:
lessons.p2: To add a lesson, create a new file with the next number in a module (e.g. {example}), start with a top-level heading, and write in Markdown. Use {h2} for sections — they become the table of contents. Keep it practical and example-led.
lessons.p3: To fix a small typo, just use the {edit} link at the bottom of any lesson — it opens a GitHub edit form.

frontmatter.intro: Each lesson starts with a YAML frontmatter block:
frontmatter.p1: {title} and {description} are required; {video} and {interview} are optional. A new {module} also needs a {nav} (with {navTitle} and an {icon}) and a new section in the {llms} config in {config}.

translations.p1: The site ships in {languages}: English (default), Spanish, French, German, Portuguese, Japanese, Chinese, Hindi, Arabic, Russian, Bengali, and Urdu. Arabic and Urdu render right-to-left.
translations.p2: {bold} Write the lesson in English only. On the next build, a LibreTranslate server running locally translates it and writes {path} for all eleven other languages. Code blocks, SAQL, links, frontmatter keys and product names are protected and come through untouched.
translations.p2Bold: You do not translate by hand.
translations.p3: To run it yourself: {all} (only changed files), or {subset}.
translations.p4: {bold} If a sentence reads badly in your language, edit that locale's file directly and open a pull request — the pipeline only overwrites a file when its {english} source changes, so your fix survives.
translations.p4Bold: Machine translation is a starting point, not the finish line.
translations.p5: UI strings live in {path}. Add new strings to {en} only; the same run fills in the other eleven and leaves existing translations alone.

submit.p1: Found a helpful link — docs, a course, a tool, a community? {link}. Title, URL and a line on why it is worth someone's time; it lands as pending and a maintainer approves it. No GitHub account, no pull request, no waiting for a build.
submit.p2: Opening an issue still works if you prefer it, and so does a pull request adding a file to {path}. The form is simply faster, and it is the same moderation queue at the other end.

code.raw: {path} — the raw-markdown surface for AI agents and crawlers.
code.p2: Style rules are enforced by ESLint: no trailing commas, 1TBS braces, 2-space indent, and one interface member per line. Run {cmd} to auto-format. Match the surrounding code's conventions.

stack.intro: The whole site is open source — here's what powers it:
stack.content: {name} — lessons authored in Markdown, served from SQLite
stack.i18n: {name} — 12 languages, eleven of them machine-translated from English
stack.hosting: {workers} + {actions} — prerendered pages served as static assets, a Worker for the dynamic routes, auto-deployed on push to {main}
stack.extras: Also in the box: {og} (social cards), {llms} (machine-readable docs), and structured data for SEO.
stack.noDb: Every lesson is prerendered at build time from Markdown, so you can write and preview lessons with {bold}. Accounts and progress run on Neon Postgres and only matter if you are working on those features — the README covers them.

pr.commit: {bold} with a clear message and {push} to your fork.
pr.open: {bold} against {main}, describing what changed and why.
pr.after: A maintainer will review, suggest tweaks if needed, and merge. Once merged, the GitHub Actions workflow builds the site and publishes it to Cloudflare automatically.

contribute.help: Stuck or have an idea? Open an issue or a discussion on {github}. First-time contributors are very welcome — no contribution is too small.

seo.title: Privacy Policy
seo.description: How CRM Analytics Academy handles your data: what an account stores, our first-party analytics, Google AdSense advertising, and how to delete it all.

hero.lead: CRM Analytics Academy is a free curriculum, funded by advertising. Here is exactly what it stores and what the ads do.

privacy.englishPrevails: This policy is machine-translated from English. If the two versions differ, the English version prevails. {link}

sections.title: What we collect
sections.body: Reading a lesson needs no account. When you visit, we record the page, how long it was open, your country (from Cloudflare), your device type, browser and operating system, and the site that referred you. We do not store your IP address. Our own analytics uses no cookies; the advertising described below does.

sections.title: Accounts
sections.body: If you create an account we store your name, email address and password hash (through Neon Auth), and what you do here: lessons completed, quiz scores, saved lessons, comments and submissions. That is what powers your dashboard, streak and badges.

sections.title: How analytics works
sections.body: Analytics is first-party: it is collected by this site, stored in our own database and read only by the site owner. A random visitor id is kept in your browser's local storage so repeat visits are counted once; clearing site data resets it. No data is sold or shared with advertisers.

sections.title: Advertising — Google AdSense
sections.body: Every lesson is free because the site shows ads from Google AdSense. Google and its partners may use cookies (including the DoubleClick cookie) to show ads based on your visits to this and other sites. You can turn off personalised advertising in Google's Ads Settings, or opt out of third-party vendor cookies at www.aboutads.info. There is nothing to buy on this site.

sections.title: Third-party links and videos
sections.body: Lessons link out to Salesforce documentation, Trailhead and community resources, and some embed YouTube videos. Those sites have their own privacy practices; a YouTube video loads only when you play it.

sections.title: Children's privacy
sections.body: This site is not directed at children under 13 and we do not knowingly collect data from them.

sections.title: Deleting your data
sections.body: Open an issue on the project's GitHub repository or message the author, and your account and everything linked to it will be deleted.

sections.title: Changes to this policy
sections.body: This policy may be updated as the project evolves. Material changes will be reflected on this page.

sections.title: Contact
sections.body: Questions about this policy? Open an issue on the project's GitHub repository.

saql.title: SAQL visualiser
saql.card: Build a query from load, filter, group, cogroup, foreach, order and limit, then watch the stream after every line.
saql.lead: Build a query, or start from an example, and step through it line by line. Every statement shows the stream it received and the stream it handed on.
saql.seoTitle: SAQL visualiser: step through a CRM Analytics query
saql.seoDesc: Watch SAQL execute line by line: load, filter, group, cogroup with inner, left, right and full joins, foreach, order and limit, on real rows.

explain.load: Loads the dataset {name}: {n} rows, {cols} fields. Nothing is filtered or grouped yet — every later line works on this stream.
explain.filter: Keeps the rows where {field} passes the test: {kept} kept, {dropped} dropped. Filtering before a group means fewer rows to group, which is why it usually comes first.
explain.group: Groups the stream by {by}: {n} rows fall into {groups} groups. Nothing is added up yet — a grouped stream holds the rows until foreach says what to compute.
explain.groupAll: Puts all {n} rows into a single group, so foreach can compute totals across everything.
explain.cogroup_inner: Cogroups on {by} = {withBy}. {keys} keys appear on either side; an inner cogroup keeps only the {kept} found on both sides and drops {dropped}.
explain.cogroup_left: Left cogroup on {by} = {withBy}: every key from the left side is kept, with or without a match — {kept} of {keys} keys, {dropped} dropped.
explain.cogroup_right: Right cogroup on {by} = {withBy}: every key from the right side is kept — {kept} of {keys} keys, {dropped} dropped.
explain.cogroup_full: Full outer cogroup on {by} = {withBy}: every key from either side is kept, matched or not — all {kept} keys.
explain.foreach: Projects each row into {cols} fields, keeping {n} rows.
explain.foreachCollapse: Computes {cols} fields for each group, so every group becomes one row: {n} rows out. This is the line where totals, counts and averages appear.
explain.order: Sorts the stream by {field}, {dir}. The rows are the same — only their order changes.
explain.limit: Keeps the first {n} rows and drops the rest. Without an order before it, which rows survive is not defined.
explain.filterGrouped: SAQL cannot filter a grouped stream. Filter before the group, or run foreach first and filter its result — that is how a HAVING is written in SAQL.
explain.groupTwice: This stream is already grouped. Run foreach first, then group its result.
explain.cogroupGrouped: Cogroup works on ungrouped streams. Move it before the group.
explain.foreachEmpty: A foreach needs at least one field.
explain.foreachAggUngrouped: {field} uses an aggregate, but the stream is not grouped. Add a group before this foreach, or group by all.
explain.foreachNotKey: {field} is not a group key, so foreach cannot project it as it is — wrap it in an aggregate such as first, sum or count.
explain.orderGrouped: Order a grouped stream after foreach, when each group is one row.
explain.limitGrouped: Limit a grouped stream after foreach.

order.title: Top to bottom
order.body: Each SAQL line takes the stream from the line before and hands on a new one. The engine may optimise, but what you read is the order the result is defined in.

group.title: Group, then foreach
group.body: Group only sorts rows into buckets. Foreach turns each bucket into one row, and only then can you filter, order or limit by a total.

cogroup.title: Cogroup is a join by key
cogroup.body: Both sides are grouped by their key and paired. Inner keeps keys on both sides; left, right and full keep the unmatched keys too, with empty values.

saql.shareHint: The address bar keeps your query: copy it to share exactly this query at this step.

recipe.title: Recipe visualiser
recipe.card: A Data Prep recipe as a graph: every join type, formula and date function, window functions, append and aggregate, in execution order.
recipe.lead: Pick an example, change any node — the join type, the keys, the formulas — and step through the recipe in the order it runs, with each node’s rows.
recipe.seoTitle: Recipe visualiser: CRM Analytics Data Prep joins, functions and execution order
recipe.seoDesc: Step through a CRM Analytics recipe: lookup, left, right, inner and outer joins with row counts, date and text formula functions, window functions, append and aggregate.
recipe.graph: Recipe graph — the number is the execution order
recipe.addFromCatalogue: Add more functions from the catalogue below.
recipe.catalogueTitle: Every formula, run on a real row

explain.input: Reads {name}: {n} rows. Inputs run first — nothing downstream can start until its inputs have.
explain.filter: Keeps rows where {field} passes the test: {kept} kept, {dropped} dropped.
explain.transform: Adds {n} calculated columns, one function at a time, in the order listed — a later formula can use an earlier one. The row count never changes in a transform.
explain.join_lookup: Lookup on {key}: every left row is kept exactly once and takes the first match. {left} rows in, {out} out — a lookup can never multiply rows. {unmatched} left rows found no match and got empty values.
explain.join_left: Left join on {key}: every left row is kept, and a row with several matches is repeated once per match. {left} rows in, {out} out; {unmatched} without a match.
explain.join_right: Right join on {key}: every right row is kept; left rows without a match are dropped. {out} rows out; {unmatchedRight} right rows had no left partner.
explain.join_inner: Inner join on {key}: only rows with a match on both sides. {left} left rows in, {out} out; {unmatched} left rows dropped.
explain.join_outer: Full outer join on {key}: every row from both sides, matched where possible. {out} rows out; {unmatched} left and {unmatchedRight} right rows without a partner.
explain.append: Stacks the inputs one under the other: {parts} rows make {n}. Columns are matched by name.
explain.aggregate: Groups {n} rows by {by} into {groups} rows and computes the measures. The grain changes here — one row per group.
explain.output: Writes {n} rows with {cols} columns to the dataset {name}. The output runs last.
explain.drop: Drops {n} columns ({fields}) from every row: the rows stay, they just get narrower, so the next node has less to move.

order.title: Order of execution
order.body: A node runs once every node it reads from has run. Branches that do not depend on each other can run in any order; the result is the same.

joins.title: Choose the join by the grain
joins.body: Lookup keeps the left grain and never adds rows. Left, inner and outer joins repeat a row for every match — check the row count after every join.

grain.title: Transform before you aggregate
grain.body: Window functions and formulas see individual rows. After an aggregate, only the group-level values are left.

dataflow.title: Dataflow visualiser
dataflow.card: A dataflow’s JSON beside its graph: digest, augment, computeExpression, computeRelative, flatten and register, run in dependency waves.
dataflow.lead: Switch nodes on and off and watch the JSON, the graph and the data change together. Step through the order the dataflow runs in.
dataflow.seoTitle: Dataflow visualiser: CRM Analytics dataflow JSON and execution order
dataflow.seoDesc: See how a CRM Analytics dataflow runs: sfdcDigest, filter, augment with LookupSingleValue or LookupMultiValue, computeExpression, computeRelative, flatten, sliceDataset and sfdcRegister with a security predicate.
dataflow.graph: Dataflow graph — W is the wave
dataflow.wavesNote: Nodes in the same wave depend on nothing in that wave, so they can run in parallel. The order of keys in the JSON does not matter.

explain.sfdcDigest: Extracts {n} rows of {object} from Salesforce, with the {fields} fields listed. Digests have no sources, so they all run in the first wave.
explain.filter: Applies {filter}: {kept} rows kept, {dropped} dropped. In dataflow filter syntax, N means not equal.
explain.augmentSingle: Augments on {key}: each of the {left} left rows takes the selected fields from its match. Augment always keeps every left row once; {unmatched} found no match.
explain.augmentSingleWarn: Augments on {key}, but {multi} left rows have more than one match. LookupSingleValue then keeps just one of them, and which one is not defined — the number can change between runs.
explain.augmentMulti: LookupMultiValue on {key}: when a left row has several matches, their values are kept together in a multi-value field. Still one row per left row; {multi} rows have several matches.
explain.computeExpression: Adds {n} fields calculated from each row on its own, with SAQL expressions.
explain.computeRelative: Adds fields that look at other rows in the same partition ({partition}, ordered by {order}): the previous deal’s amount and the first close date.
explain.flatten: Turns the manager hierarchy into a list of every manager above each user, and a path. Security predicates use it so managers see their team’s rows.
explain.sliceDataset: Drops {fields} from the dataset — fields nobody needs, or that must not be exposed.
explain.register: Registers {n} rows as the dataset {alias}. Without a predicate, anyone with access to the app sees every row.
explain.registerSecure: Registers {n} rows as {alias} with the security predicate {predicate}: each user sees only rows owned by them or by people who report to them.

order.title: Dependencies, not position
order.body: A node runs when its sources have. That is why digests run together first and register runs last, wherever they sit in the JSON.

augment.title: Augment never adds rows
augment.body: Put the grain you want on the left. Single value picks one match; multi value keeps all of them in one field. Neither repeats the left row.

recipes.title: Dataflows and recipes
recipes.body: Recipes are the newer tool and do the same jobs with joins, formulas and a visual editor. Dataflows still run in many orgs — read both.

joins.title: Joins visualiser
joins.card: One join, one row at a time: lines to every match, what each join type keeps, fan-out, and the rows nothing matched.
joins.seoTitle: CRM Analytics recipe joins, visualised: lookup, left, right, inner and outer

joins.empty: Nothing yet: step through the left rows.

what.lookup: Lookup: every left row once, with its first match or empty.
what.left: Left: every left row, repeated once per match, empty when none.
what.right: Right: every right row, with its matches; left rows with no match are dropped.
what.inner: Inner: only rows that match on both sides.
what.outer: Outer: everything from both sides, matched where it can be.

fate.joined: {row}: {key} = {value} finds one match, so the row joins.
fate.fanout: {row}: {key} = {value} finds {n} matches, so the row appears {n} times.
fate.lookupFirst: {row}: {key} = {value} finds {n} matches; lookup takes only the first.
fate.leftOnly: {row}: {key} = {value} finds no match; the row is kept with an empty right side.
fate.dropped: {row}: {key} = {value} finds no match, so this join drops it.

joins.rightKept: {n} {side} rows matched nothing; this join keeps them with an empty left side.
joins.rightDropped: {n} {side} rows matched nothing and are left out. {total} rows in the output.

use.lookup: you want to add the Account’s name and region to every Opportunity, without ever duplicating an Opportunity.
use.left: you want every Account with all of its Opportunities, and still see Accounts that have none.
use.right: the right side is what you must keep: every Account, whether or not an Opportunity points at it.
use.inner: you only care about records that exist on both sides, like Opportunities whose Account is known.
use.outer: you are reconciling two systems and need to see what is missing on either side.

bindings.title: Bindings visualiser
bindings.card: Click a chart and follow the selection into another query: column(), cell(), asObject, asString, asEquality, and the SAQL they write.
bindings.seoTitle: CRM Analytics bindings, visualised: selection and result bindings step by step
bindings.seoDesc: See how a CRM Analytics dashboard binding works: a selection or result, column() or cell(), asObject, asString or asEquality, and the SAQL it rewrites.
bindings.clickHint: Click a bar to select it.
bindings.resultHint: A result binding reads the whole result: here, the first row.

say.source: The binding starts from stage_1.{kind}: the rows behind {values}.
say.data: column() pulls the StageName values out of those rows (cell() would take one value).
say.serialise: .{ser}() turns the values into text SAQL can read.
say.inject: The {mustache} in q_deals is replaced by that text before the query is sent.
say.run: q_deals runs again with the new filter: {n} rows.

bindings.brokenNote: asString joins several values into one string that no row equals, so nothing comes back. Use asObject or asEquality for multiple values.

what.title: What a binding is
what.body: A binding is a {mustache} expression inside a query or a widget property. Before the query runs, the dashboard replaces it with text taken from another step.

selection.title: Selection binding
selection.body: Reads what the user selected in another step. It changes every time they click.

result.title: Result binding
result.body: Reads the result of another step, for example its first row, whether or not anything is selected.

asObject.title: asObject()
asObject.body: Writes the values as SAQL literals: a list from column(), one value from cell().

asString.title: asString()
asString.body: Writes plain text with no quotes. Good for one value inside a string you build yourself; wrong for several values.

asEquality.title: asEquality(field)
asEquality.body: Writes a whole condition, field == value or field in [values], ready for a filter.

faceting.title: Bindings or faceting?
faceting.body: Faceting filters every step on the same dataset with no code. Bindings are for other datasets, or for changing measures, groupings and properties.

fn.year: Takes the year out of a date.
fn.quarter: Gives the quarter of the year, 1 to 4.
fn.day: Gives the day of the month.
fn.day_of_week: Gives the day of the week, 1 (Sunday) to 7 (Saturday).
fn.week: Gives the ISO week of the year.
fn.date_trunc_month: Moves a date back to the first day of its month, so dates group by month.
fn.add_months: Adds a number of months to a date, for renewals and due dates.
fn.date_diff_days: Counts the days between two dates.
fn.days_until_today: Counts the days from a date to today: how old a record is.
fn.last_day: Gives the last day of the date’s month.
fn.to_date: Turns text in a known format into a real date, so date functions and date filters work on it.
fn.substr: Takes part of a text, by position and length.
fn.length: Counts the characters in a text.
fn.replace: Replaces every match of one text with another.
fn.round: Rounds a number; a negative position rounds to tens, hundreds or thousands.
fn.multiply: Multiplies a number, for tax, currency or margin.
fn.abs: Removes the sign of a number.
fn.coalesce: Gives the first value that is not null: a default for missing values.
fn.bucket: Sorts values into named ranges with case when.
fn.case_won: Turns a condition into 1 or 0, so it can be summed.
fn.is_null: Tells missing values apart from present ones.
fn.running_total: Adds up a column row after row, in order, restarting for every partition.
fn.rank: Numbers rows by a value inside their partition: 1 is the highest.
fn.lag: Reads the value from the previous row in the partition.
fn.share_of_partition: Gives each row’s share of its partition’s total, in percent.

security.title: Security predicate visualiser
security.card: Pick who is logged in and watch row-level security decide, row by row, what they can see.
security.seoTitle: CRM Analytics security predicates, visualised: row-level security step by step
security.seoDesc: See how a CRM Analytics security predicate works: $User.Id is filled in, every row is checked against the owner and the manager hierarchy, and only matching rows reach the dashboard.
security.noPredicate: No predicate: everyone sees every row
security.atQuery: When the dashboard queries the dataset
security.step0: {name} opens the dashboard. Before any row is read, $User.Id in the predicate becomes their user id.

why.none: visible: the dataset has no predicate.
why.team: visible: {owner} reports to them, so they are in the row’s ManagerChain.
why.teamOff: hidden: {owner} reports to them, but this predicate only checks the owner.
why.no: hidden: {owner} owns it and they are not in that row’s ManagerChain.

what.title: What a security predicate is
what.body: A filter stored on the dataset. CRM Analytics adds it to every query on that dataset, for every user, before any dashboard filter. A row that fails it never reaches the dashboard.

user.title: $User fields
user.body: $User.Id, $User.UserRoleId and other $User fields are replaced with the logged-in user’s values when the query runs, so one predicate gives each person their own rows.

flatten.title: Hierarchies need a flatten
flatten.body: To let managers see their team, a recipe or dataflow flattens the role or manager hierarchy into a multi-value field (here ManagerChain). The predicate then checks whether the user is anywhere in it.

sharing.title: Predicate or sharing inheritance?
sharing.body: Sharing inheritance copies Salesforce sharing for supported objects. A predicate is for everything else, or when you want a simpler rule.
